These exercises practise the ideas from Chapter 1: using R as a calculator, storing values in objects, calling functions, and taking a first look at Elaf's data.

Edit the code in any box and press **Run Code**. R runs in your browser, so the first run can take a few seconds while R starts. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

## Warming up with a few numbers

### Exercise 1: R as a calculator

Elaf kept a note of how long she slept on three nights: 6.5, 7, and 5.5 hours. Use R to work out her average sleep. Then try changing the numbers.


::: {.cell exercise='ex1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
(6.5 + 7 + 5.5) / 3
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
(6.5 + 7 + 5.5) / 3
```

R follows the usual order of operations, so the brackets matter. Without them, R divides only 5.5 by 3: try `6.5 + 7 + 5.5 / 3`.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: Storing values in an object

Store the numbers in an object called `sleep` with `c()`, which combines values, then use `mean()`. Add a fourth night of 8 hours. What happens to the average?


::: {.cell exercise='ex2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
sleep <- c(6.5, 7, 5.5)
sleep
mean(sleep)
```
:::


::: { .hint exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Add the new value inside `c()`, separated by a comma: `c(6.5, 7, 5.5, ______)`.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
sleep <- c(6.5, 7, 5.5, 8)
sleep
mean(sleep)
```

The average rises from 6.33 to 6.75 hours.
:::
:::

### Exercise 3: More functions

Find the shortest and longest night and the number of nights, then round the average to one decimal place.


::: {.cell exercise='ex3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
sleep <- c(6.5, 7, 5.5, 8)
min(sleep)
______(sleep)
______(sleep)
round(mean(sleep), ______)
```
:::


::: { .hint exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The functions you need are `max()` and `length()`. The second argument of `round()` is the number of decimal places.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
sleep <- c(6.5, 7, 5.5, 8)
min(sleep)
max(sleep)
length(sleep)
round(mean(sleep), 1)
```
:::
:::

## Elaf's data

Now the same ideas on the real case study. The file `students.csv` has one row for each of the 600 students in Elaf's study.

### Exercise 4: Opening the data

Read the file into an object called `students`. How many students (rows) and variables (columns) are there? Use `head()` to see the first six rows.


::: {.cell exercise='ex4'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
students <- read.csv("students.csv")
nrow(students)
ncol(students)
head(students)
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
students <- read.csv("students.csv")
nrow(students)   # 600 students
ncol(students)   # 14 variables
head(students)
names(students)  # the names of all the variables
```
:::
:::

### Exercise 5: A first question, and a first surprise

What is the average age of the students? The `$` sign picks one column from the data. Run the code first as it is: the answer is `NA`, which means "not available". One student's age is missing, and R will not guess. Fill in the blank so that R ignores the missing value.


::: {.cell setup='true' exercise='["ex5","ex6"]'}
```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex5, ex6]
students <- read.csv("students.csv")
```
:::



::: {.cell exercise='ex5'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
mean(students$age)
mean(students$age, ______)
```
:::


::: { .hint exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

`mean()` has an argument called `na.rm`, short for "NA remove".
:::
:::

::: { .hint exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

Set it to `TRUE`: `mean(students$age, na.rm = ______)`.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean(students$age, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(students$age))   # how many ages are missing
```

`na.rm = TRUE` tells R to remove missing values before calculating.
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: Counting

`table()` counts how many times each value appears. How many students come from each faculty? Then find out how many were invited to the wellbeing workshop (the variable is called `workshop`).


::: {.cell exercise='ex6'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
table(students$faculty)
table(students$______)
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
table(students$faculty)
table(students$workshop)
```

Exactly half the students, 300, were invited: the invitation was random.
:::
:::

### Challenge: Your first plot

Elaf's semester records are in `semesters.csv`. Draw a histogram of how many hours students sleep with `hist()`. Can you add a title with the `main` argument?


::: {.cell exercise='ex7'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex7
semesters <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
hist(semesters$sleep_hours)
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex7" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
semesters <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
hist(semesters$sleep_hours,
     main = "How long do graduate students sleep?",
     xlab = "Hours of sleep per night")
```
:::
:::

## Work on your own computer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Download the Chapter 1 project

The project contains the data, these exercises, and their solutions, ready to open in RStudio.

- [Download chapter01.zip](chapter01.zip), unzip it, and double-click `chapter01.Rproj`.
- Or type this one line in RStudio's Console to download, unzip, and open it:

```r
usethis::use_course("https://polla-fattah.github.io/R4NTR/playground/chapter01.zip")
```

If R says there is no package called `usethis`, install it first with `install.packages("usethis")`.
:::
